title: Debugging Tools & Techniques
summary: Reading code only gets you so far. Learn the practical toolkit — interactive debuggers, git bisect, sanitizers, and time-travel debugging — and when each one actually earns its setup cost.

slides.markdown:
[systematic-debugging-method](systematic-debugging-method) gives you the loop; [reading-stack-traces-and-logs](reading-stack-traces-and-logs) gives you the observation. This topic is the toolkit that speeds up every step in between — forming and testing hypotheses faster than adding another print statement and rerunning.

No single tool wins everywhere. An interactive debugger is overkill for a one-line typo and irreplaceable for a corrupted data structure three calls deep. `git bisect` finds a regressing commit in minutes that would take an afternoon of manual review. Sanitizers catch memory bugs that would otherwise surface as a crash weeks later, in a different function entirely.

The skill is matching the tool to the bug, and knowing which tools simply aren't available once code reaches production — which sets up the next topic.

slides.subTitle: Breakpoints, stepping, watch expressions, call-stack inspection
slides.markdown:
An interactive debugger (`pdb`, `gdb`, Chrome DevTools, an IDE's built-in debugger) pauses your program mid-execution and lets you inspect it, rather than inferring state from what you thought to print in advance.

The core moves:

- **Breakpoints** — pause execution at a specific line, unconditionally.
- **Stepping** — advance one line (step over), or step into a function call to follow it.
- **Watch expressions** — flag a variable or expression and get notified the instant it changes, even across many lines of execution.
- **Call-stack inspection** — jump to any frame currently on the stack and inspect *its* local variables, not just the one you're paused in.

The advantage over print statements: you can inspect *any* variable in scope after the fact, not just the ones you thought to log, and you can change a value live to test a hypothesis without editing and rerunning code.

slides.sectionTitle: Print vs debugger vs static analysis
slides.markdown:
| Technique | Best for | Weakness |
|---|---|---|
| **Print/log debugging** | Distributed systems, timing-sensitive bugs, quick sanity checks | Need to guess what to log in advance; edit-rerun cycle is slow |
| **Interactive debugger** | Deep single-process bugs, unfamiliar codebases, inspecting full state | Can alter timing (breaks race conditions), awkward across processes/services |
| **Static analysis** | Catching a whole class of bug before it ever runs (null derefs, type errors, unused results) | Can't tell you about *this specific* runtime failure — no execution, no live state |

None of these is strictly superior. A race condition that vanishes the instant you attach a debugger (the **probe effect**, covered later in this group) is a case where print/log debugging is the *only* viable option, not a fallback. A linter catching "you never check this function's return value" prevents a bug you'd otherwise chase for an hour later — that's static analysis winning before debugging even starts.

A plain breakpoint stops on *every* pass through a line — useless if a loop runs 50,000 times and the bug is on iteration 4,982. Two refinements solve this:

- **Conditional breakpoints** stop only when an expression is true — `user_id == 884 and retries > 2`. The debugger evaluates it silently on every pass and only interrupts you when it matches.
- **Logpoints** (a.k.a. tracepoints) print an expression's value each time the line executes, *without* stopping — you get a targeted log stream for exactly the state you care about, without editing source to add a print statement and without redeploying.

Both exist because "the bug only happens under specific state" is the common case, not the exception — most real bugs aren't on the first iteration or the obvious path, and a breakpoint that fires unconditionally on a hot loop is worse than useless.

slides.sectionTitle: git bisect to find a regression
slides.markdown:
When you know a commit range contains a regression but not which commit, `git bisect` automates the binary search from [systematic-debugging-method](systematic-debugging-method) over your commit history:

```bash
git bisect start
git bisect bad HEAD           # current commit is broken
git bisect good v2.3.0        # this old tag was known-good
# git checks out the midpoint commit automatically

# run your repro/test, then tell git the result:
git bisect bad                # still broken -> narrows to the newer half
# ...repeat...
git bisect good                # fixed here -> narrows to the older half

# eventually:
# abc1234 is the first bad commit
git bisect reset
```

With `git bisect run <test-command>`, this fully automates: git checks out each midpoint, runs your test script, reads its exit code, and continues the search with zero manual judgment calls. A 1,000-commit range resolves in about 10 steps — turning an afternoon of `git log` archaeology into a five-minute automated search.

A normal debugger only moves forward: step, and the past is gone. **Record-replay debugging** (tools like `rr`, or time-travel debugging in some IDEs) records a full execution trace once, then lets you replay it and step **backward** as many times as you want — including "run to here, then tell me the last time this variable changed."

This matters most for bugs where the failure is far downstream of the cause: a corrupted value discovered at line 400 that was actually written wrong at line 40, twenty function calls earlier. Without replay, finding that requires re-running the whole program repeatedly with breakpoints creeping backward one guess at a time. With replay, you record once and can jump straight to "the last write to this address" — turning a multi-hour hunt into a single query.

The cost is recording overhead and tooling that isn't available for every language and platform, which is why it's a specialist tool reached for on the hardest bugs rather than a daily default.

slides.subTitle: Sanitizers and leak detectors for native code
slides.markdown:
Languages without automatic memory management (C, C++, and native extensions in other languages) have a whole bug category that memory-managed languages mostly don't: use-after-free, buffer overruns, double-frees, and leaks. These often don't crash where the mistake happens — they corrupt memory silently and crash somewhere unrelated, much later.

**Sanitizers** (AddressSanitizer, MemorySanitizer, UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer) instrument the binary at compile time to catch these at the exact moment they occur, not when the corruption finally causes a visible crash. **Leak detectors** (Valgrind's memcheck, LeakSanitizer) track every allocation and report what was never freed at program exit.

The trade-off is overhead — sanitized binaries commonly run 2–10x slower — so they're a testing/CI tool, not a production one. Running your test suite under AddressSanitizer regularly is one of the highest-value/lowest-effort things a native-code team can do, because it turns a bug that would surface as a baffling crash into a precise stack trace at the actual mistake.

slides.sectionTitle: Dev vs staging vs production tooling
slides.markdown:
| Environment | Tooling available | Stakes of a mistake |
|---|---|---|
| **Dev** | Full debugger, breakpoints, arbitrary logging, can pause indefinitely | Low — only affects you |
| **Staging** | Usually a debugger attachable, synthetic or sampled data | Low-medium — shared, but not customer-facing |
| **Production** | Rarely a debugger; logs, metrics, traces, maybe a read-only shell | High — real users, real money, real data |

The tooling gap is the whole reason production debugging is its own discipline, covered next: you cannot pause a live process serving real traffic to single-step through it the way you would locally, and even where you technically *can* attach a debugger to a production process, pausing it has a blast radius — every request it's holding stalls.

The practical implication: build the observability (logs, metrics, traces) that substitutes for a debugger *before* the incident, not during it.

slides.sectionTitle: Debug code left in a shipped commit
slides.markdown:
A debugging session often leaves traces: a `print("HERE!!!")`, a hardcoded test user ID that bypasses a permission check, a feature flag flipped locally to skip an expensive call, an env var override. Left uncommitted, these are harmless. Committed and shipped, they range from embarrassing to a security hole.

Real patterns this causes:

- A debug endpoint that dumps internal state, left reachable in production because it was only meant to be temporary.
- A bypassed auth check ("just to test the happy path") that ships and grants unintended access.
- Verbose debug logging left on, silently leaking the sensitive data covered in the previous topic, or drowning real signal in noise.

The fix isn't just discipline — it's process: a PR checklist item, a linter rule that flags known debug patterns (`console.log`, `pdb.set_trace()`, `TODO: remove`), and treating "did you review your own diff before requesting review" as a real step, not a formality.

slides.sectionTitle: Matching the tool to the bug
slides.markdown:
A rough decision guide, built from the trade-offs above:

- **"Which commit broke this?"** → `git bisect`, especially with `git bisect run` if you have an automatable test.
- **"What's the state of this object right now?"** → interactive debugger with a conditional breakpoint at the right line.
- **"This only happens on iteration 4,982 of a loop."** → conditional breakpoint or logpoint, not a plain one.
- **"The bug disappears when I attach a debugger."** → you're likely looking at a timing-sensitive bug; switch to logging or a record-replay tool instead.
- **"The crash is way downstream of the actual mistake."** → record-replay if available, otherwise binary-search backward with logging.
- **"Native code crashes intermittently with no clear cause."** → run under a sanitizer before anything else.

Picking the wrong tool doesn't just waste time — an interactive debugger on a race condition can actively hide the bug by changing its timing, which is exactly what the next topic is about.

slides.sectionTitle: Tooling is leverage, not a substitute
slides.markdown:
Every tool in this topic makes one step of the debugging loop faster — observing state, narrowing the search space, testing a hypothesis. None of them replaces the loop itself. A debugger in the hands of someone shotgun-debugging just lets them thrash faster and with more confidence, stepping through code without a specific question they're trying to answer.

The useful habit: before reaching for any tool, name the question it's supposed to answer — "what is the value of this field the instant before it's read" or "which commit introduced this" — and only then pick the tool built for that question. A breakpoint set without a question in mind is just an expensive way to stare at code.

This toolkit assumes you can attach to the running process — true in dev, often true in staging, rarely true in production. The next topic, [production-debugging-observability](production-debugging-observability), covers the workflow when most of these tools simply aren't options: no breakpoints, no stepping, no live inspection, just the logs, metrics, and traces you instrumented in advance.

And the probe-effect problem introduced above — a tool changing the very behavior it's trying to observe — gets a full topic of its own next in [concurrency-bugs-and-heisenbugs](concurrency-bugs-and-heisenbugs), because it's the defining challenge of debugging concurrent code.
